blocks.x: Stop it Paul, she can't fix it. Okay. Alright. What's your name? My name is Joseph. That's not what everybody calls you. They call me Kid Twat from the Boothwaite.

Well where the Boothwaite come from? I was up in St. Paul, Minnesota. I left there. I came on down there to St. Louis. Where I was then. They used me. I was taken right from my own hometown. And then what they call me then? Kid Twat from the Boothwaite. Why they call me that? Because I was a cigarette tester. Cigarette tester. Where were you born? I was born right here on the next street. I was right there where I came out. In Algiers. Al J is right where I am young now. On the next street I'm on the Homer Street and the next street is Newton. And I still live there. And where were you? What year? I was born in 1907. Exact day? Oh man. I can't cause for Louis Armstrong. Red Allen. We all played together. This is how I told you before. And them boys is going to let me. Why? I didn't have a daddy to do. Teach me. When I first bought my bass. What he did. He shot at me with his shotgun. But he skipped me. Ha ha. He skipped me. Cause I was ducking. I wanted that way. I paid my money off. I was waiting for tuition water board. And boy I was getting $12 a week. I mean $21.60 a week. One week I give my mama $60. And the next week I give my mama $11. And I keep the $10.60. Next week I keep the $10.60. You see? But old Red Allen was playing. You couldn't hear him when he was playing. They call him Biffley. They call him Biffley. And then we used to sit on the corner. We used to look at him coming. And then he'd say. I said. I said. Look at the old man coming. He said. Let him come a little closer. Let him come a little closer. Everybody take me for Louis. Yeah. Louis is my cousin. And anytime Louis come anywhere around the city. The area of New Orleans. He'd come and see twat from the bourgeois. Why'd he call me twat from the bourgeois? Because I was up in St. Louis. And he was brought down.
You told us that once.

Well I told you that once. Because I tell you why. They used to call me Turk. Turkey Buzzard. Turkey Buzzard. Why? I used to name him Dark and Hansel. But man when I started to pick on that bass. Them cats let me go. I used to sit down. Everybody used to play the piano. I said. Now I'm going to get me something different. I said. Let me play a little piece once in a while. He said. No man. I said. I just got you. Well I said. I'm going to get me something to myself. I got on and I prayed. I said. Lord. What can I get for them guys who keep from knowing me. And I started to. And I made me a little string. They come. Toot. Toot. Toot. Toot. And I used to hold bass for Louis. I'm. Oh. Chris Kelly and all them. Still get rang. And old. All them boys right now. I don't know what they call them.
When did you start with Thomas. When did you start with Thomas.

I start with Thomas. When Thomas come here. I didn't go get him. He came here to me. And he came here around in 19 and. Around in 15. And that's when you started. Around in the 1915. September storm. Right about a year after that. I can't remember. Because when this cat come through here with that. I had a little brother. And he used to beat on a tube. You know. And this cat here used to be. Thomas. I was. Boy. My brother. He died. You know. And I said. We was going to be some great musicians. I said. We ain't going to stay around. Yeah. And I said. I didn't know where I was going. But I said. We're not going to stay around. Yeah. But my brother died. And so. Young come Thomas. And he was living a few blocks from me. And I heard that cat blow. I said. That's the cat. Where he at? And I went underneath his house. You see. And then. And I. I. I. I. I. I. Put my clothes. My ear so close to up underneath his house. So he stopped playing. I say. He must be. See. I'm going to need this house. You know. I might be a dog or anything. You know. But I. He said. I'm a dog. You know. I self. You know. So I said. Well. Look. Yeah. They done stopped playing. I wanted to know. I'm under this house. And he said. He started again. Da da da da da da da da da. And I said. Ah. They going again. And boy. I mean. I went and bought me a bass. I paid. Six dollars on it to where I got me.
We got to give Sammy Penn a chance now. Okay.
Well. No. Sammy Penn. Only chance Sammy Penn got. He was on his own. Because I'm a good boy.

Fall off. Yeah. Okay. When were you born? I was born in September. September the 15th. 1902. And where? In Morgan City, Louisiana. And did you play any music out there at all? That's where I started at. I started playing in Morgan City. When I started playing music. It's a funny thing to tell you. What I'm going to tell you. I started. I had one of those cheese boxes. For snare drum. And a white tub. They call it. For a bass drum. And a fellow made me some springs. For a pedal. Made a pedal. That's how I started in Morgan City. Played with a band by the name. Allen's band. Allen? And I started playing with one of the famous big bands there. They're called Ezekiel Mack. From Morgan City, Louisiana. And did your family play at all? No. I had a son. Liked to play the saxophone. He changed. Changed to a tram on. And he quit playing. When did you come to the city? Oh, I've been to the city now about 20 some years. You played with some great bands after your family. I did. And after I stopped playing Chris Kelly, I played with several big bands in the city. Most of them is dead now. Did you ever know Buddy Petit? Yes. Must have been here in the 20s. 1920s. Something like that. Yeah, I see. How long have you been with Thomas? About 30 some years. About 32 years. Who are some of your favorite drummers? Oh, I had a couple of good drummers that died here in the city of New Orleans. I met since I've been here. Was the famous, which was this boy, Chani. And another great drummer died here in New Orleans that I know quite a bit. I just can't call his name at the moment. Who did he play with? Oh, he played with all these big bands, Tuxedars and different bands. Was he better than Red Hattie? Well, in my way, he was just about the same. They both were good drummers. You don't remember what bands he played with, huh? Well, right now I just can't remember the bands. Did you know Henry Zeno? Yes, I remember him. Well, I can't guess a man's name anyhow. What about when you first started? Did you hear any drummers out in the country you liked? Well, they had a good band out there from Thibodeau called Garbio's Band. He had one of the best drummers I ever heard. His name was Boleg. Boleg. And I liked it the way he played. All right. I see. What about lately? Have you played with any brass bands or anything in late years? Well, no. I stopped playing brass bands about five years ago. I didn't like too much walking. What brass bands did you play with? Well, I played with E. Ricker. And I also had a tuxedo band. At that time, when I first came to the honor. Were you a regular member? Yes, I was a member. Is that the original tuxedo or young tuxedo? No, that was the original tuxedo band. Celestan and Rageley and those guys, huh? That's right. Who do you feel you play like on drums? You don't feel there's any man you copy of records or anything? Well, I'll tell you. Allen, I never did copy of nobody. I always played my own way of playing drums. Yeah. I always did. But I went out and seen and heard some nice drummers. Like the way he played. But I always did like to play my own style. And I've been doing that ever since I've been playing. Let's see. I wish you could tell me some more of the different bands you played with besides Thomas and Petit and Kelly. I played with Randy. That was one of the big bands in New Orleans. Mm-hmm. Kid Randy. I stayed with him for quite a while. And Morgan, I went out with Morgan on the lake. I played with Morgan out there. Around Gulfport. Oh, I stayed out there a long time. That's Sam? Sam Morgan. Mm-hmm. Do you play any tough spots here in town? Well, I have been in some of the best spots that you have in New Orleans. I've been around playing in some of the best places that you have in the city. Uh-huh. Such as? That's right. How's that? What are some of the places? Well, we'll call, you take at the hotels. I played at every hotel you have in New Orleans. Mostly. Roseville and different places. And of course, New Orleans, you know we all played there. Mm-hmm. And even at the jungles, I've been to all those good places. I played at this big place on Connell Street, the brass. I think they called it the brass rail at that time. I was there once. Well, I think that'll get it. Thank you very much. Thank you. Yeah. All right. What's your name? Donald Valentine. Well, how come they called you Kid Thomas? It was just band name. Oh, band name. I see. Yeah. And where were you born? St. John, Paris. Mm-hmm. In a town? No, no.
Country town.
Near Reserve? Reserve. Right in Reserve. Yeah. Oh, I see. And what year were you born?
Uh, 18... Wait, wait.
I see.
I see. And what about your family? Who played in your family? My family, my daddy. Your daddy played? What did he play?

Trombone. Oh, that's right. All right. Trombone. Play different effort. Play trumpet. Clarinet. Mm-hmm. So on like that. Well, how'd you get started in music? Well, I got started for... After my daddy had a brass band, you know.
Mm-hmm.

And all our boys got together, the hall boys, you know. We all got together. See, they used to have rehearsals. We'd go and after they finished, we'd have rehearsals the next day, you know. We'd go there and select what instrument we wanted to play, you know. So we just went on and flew on with the instrument playing. Well, we made some instruments, you know. We made a bass. We made a bass volley with some fishing line, you know. Accord, you know. Made a bass. And then we had a little kuzuk, they call them, you know. You put a little piece of silk paper in it. You play a trumpet, you know. So, and so we had a drum and so on like that, you know. And so, well, after a while, we started to feel the instrument, you know. Well, after we started to feel the instrument, I couldn't tell them about maybe one number, one at a time, you know, one number at a time. Got that in dance. After we got that in the arm, they tried another number. So after we could play my three number, so fella hired us. Have a club room over there, you know. He hired us. So we played the three numbers all night. We played the first, we played slow. Next time, we played fast. You know what I mean? Three numbers. And, well, we were beginning to get kind of good then, you know. So whatever we did, after we began getting really good, so the trumpet I had was kind of bad, my daddy gave me. So I bought my trumpet on Ramport Street. $35. All right, I was getting pretty good then. So, well, after we began to get real good, the man, he owned a drugstore. He wanted, he asked us, he said, what name you want to give, what name you want to give your band? He said, why don't you give your band the medicine, some medicine they put up itself, you know. That's what he put up, prescribed itself. They called it Niles, you know. So we named the band Niles. Niles Band, you see. It's all right. Then after we organized this band, we bought all new instruments. We bought a whole set of Horton, you know, Horton instruments, trumpet, trombone, all instruments, Horton. So, well, we began to get good then. Then we started playing a big job.
I don't mean to cut you off, but when you were a kid like that, was there anybody you listened to that was your favorite, that you might copy out of?

Well, I used to listen, I used to listen at, see, Ori, Ori, Ori band originated out there in the country, in the Platt. Mm-hmm. After they came, they came down here and lived down here, well, they used to come out there and play, you know. Mm-hmm. Ori. And, uh.
Did you know Chip?

Chip, yeah, Chip. I knew Chip, too. And, uh, it's because you come out there. I don't know what you call it. What he played? I don't know what you mean. Joe Oliver. He used to come out and play with Ori bands, you see. Uh-huh. And, uh, so, so, Jack Carey, Mud Carey, he used to come out and play, too. Mm-hmm. He came out and played with this band they had in the country. The older band was there before Washington. But after the trumpet player got drowned, well, they got him to play trumpet with them.
Well, that was Alexander drowned.

No. Yeah, yeah. Uh-huh. Yeah. So, well, it got him to play trumpet. Mm-hmm. So, but I liked it. I liked the Joe Oliver playing, you know what I mean? But I never did cop at nobody, you see. Oh, I see. I never did, you know, no patron at nobody. I played my own, my own way. We all, we all played our own way. Yeah.
When did you come to New Orleans, though?
I came to New Orleans in 20, the first war is 122, 23.
You came what, right after the war? After the war. About a year after the war.
Uh-huh, yeah, 23.
I see. Did you have a teacher in the country?
No, I had no teacher.
When I came here, I went to Manu Mineta.

Yeah, hold it. Yeah. So you went to Mineta, huh? Yeah, I went to Mineta. And I went to Mineta, so after this boy, Elton Seto, he had the band, you know, trumpet player, drank some liquor in the cannon, got poison.
Mm-hmm.

See, he dropped dead on the canal and ran port, you see. So, well, his brother-in-law told him, he said, well, I know a fella in my could get him to come down, you know what I mean? So, but I was already down here already, you see. I lived on Kyle Street, you see. So he said, you might get him. So sure enough, he written a letter to me, so he sent a letter to me. I got a letter, so he told me how to come over in the algae. I never been to algae before in my life. So I came right on over, just like he said, I came right on on Fred Street. I came right there, and his wife told me, he said, you sure find this place good. You know what I mean? For strange, you know what I mean? I came right on the couch, you know. So, well, there we, uh, he didn't have the trumpet player, well, I started playing with him, you know. And, uh, well, we wouldn't, uh, we wouldn't rehearse three and four times a week. Mm-hmm. We had a lot of jobs we could have, you know, a lot of weight, but we didn't want no jobs at all. We just wanted to rehearse and get the band together. See, so, after we got, after we got our band together, the first, the first dance I played in the algae is on Devil Street. Mm-hmm. At Devil, uh, uh, uh, uh, it was, uh, it was a, it was a corner. Uh, it was a, it was a corner. Uh, it was a, it was a corner. It wasn't a hall, it was a pavilion. And it rained all, it rained all day and all night. And from that on, we started playing. We used to go all over, play on the lake, play in the country, play in the country, Raceland, Lockport, Gold Medal, down the, the Grand Isles, all over. Timberto, Homer, all over. Baton Rouge, everywhere, man, Texas, all over, see?
Played contest? You ever had a contest?

Yeah, yeah, we had a contest. We had a contest with, uh, Sun Allen. We had this contest with Sun Allen. Well, I tell you, how we come to have this contest, we used to rehearse them. And, uh, so some of the boys heard our band, you know, say, Man, I say, I heard a band, man. I say, I hear the band, rehearse it all the time. He said, Well, a good band. You know, tell, other fellas, tell the other fellas back, you know. Ah, man, them fellas can't play nothing. That's what the other fellas said. I say, All right. I say, Now listen. So he told them, say, Well, all right. You think they can't play nothing? I say, I tell you what you do. Put some money down there and we'll give a dance. You know what I mean? Contest, back in the turtle bag, back there, you see? It's all right. Sure enough, they all got together and put the money together. Well, you must have advertised that about a month or so, or two. You know what I mean? And, uh, so that night, when the dance came off, you see? We had people like that in. All from old river, everybody. So, Sonny Allen, he had the regular bandstand, you know, to the back. And we had to build an extra bandstand to the door. You know, the entrance where you come in. So, it's all right. We play, so. So, now we, see we have to play a number, a prize number. See? So, this man playing bass with an old man, call him Wushong. He said, he said, Sonny Allen, you know something different? I said, yeah, I know something different. I said, yeah, I know something different. I used to play a waltz when I was in the country. I was playing with a band on this side of the river, after I left on the other side, you see? Red Devil, you see? So, and we used to play these waltz all the time, you know? So, I remember, I said, yeah, I said, I'm going to play that. He said, you play it. So, I played it. So, after I played it, everybody, oh man, everybody's talking about that pretty waltz. Woo! He said, that's the beautiful waltz we'll be hearing. It's all right. So, now, when we ended, that was supposed to be a prize. So, look, everybody clapped for applause, you know? So, the police were there. So, the police were there. They still, they still, the ball band standing. So, they didn't want to give me the prize, you know? They don't want to give it to them. But the police would say, oh yeah, you can give that for that prize. They said, because he wanted fair, you know what I mean? So, and from that, from that day on, I made enemies. In the island, they wouldn't hire me no more. They wouldn't hire me no more. But, but I, most of my playing was, most of white. All my playing. Most, now most of the time I would play for color, like in Lent. See, like net, like it's net now.
And brass bands too though. Yeah, brass bands too, yeah.
Played a few parades and things. But, most I played for color, in Lent, you know. And, play all of them in the world.
What are some of the brass bands you played with?
Well, I played, I played with John Catten, Brad Baird, I played with Erika Brad Baird, and so on.
Were you a regular member or just once a while?

I was a regular member in John's band. Yeah. Yeah, I just got out after them fellas man, that fellas that like the auger too much, you know what I mean? Had a fella that he like the auger, man and Gabbert, he said, I like the auger so much, you know. So, I got this guy, me and this boy Albert, you know. Told me Albert's son. Yeah, Lutcher. Lutcher. So, we got out. Not, he was playing with him, and Remus Maschews, Bill Maschews, brother, you know. So, Remus told me one day when he was coming across, he said, you know, big kid, he said, I believe I'm going to change my way of living. I said, what you mean? He said, man, I'm going to join church. I'm going to get away from this, because I'm too old to go to penitentiary, you know what I mean? You don't get in trouble, you know. He said, I feel like the auger too much. So, he got away from me and he joined the church. That's what he did. Quit playing all together, you see. So, well, after that I didn't fool with Brad Baird too much no more, you know.

We better stop here, we got to do a little with Manuel Paul. Yeah, yeah, yeah. So, thank you very much. Okay. Okay, what's your name? Emmanuel Paul. Yeah, where were you born? In New Orleans, Louisiana. Mm-hmm. And, uh, excuse me. Oh, God, I'm sorry. Uh, what year? Time, exactly. Ah, February the 2nd, 1904. Mm-hmm. Uh, did anybody in your family play music? No, no one in the family. Mm-hmm. Well, how'd you get interested in it? Well, through friends. As a youngster? As a youngster, in my teenage. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And as about 17 years old, I became a religious character there and joined church. And through the church, that's where I received my first instrument. Mm-hmm. All the young people of the church, they, uh, formed the band, you see. They were trying to make a Christian band. And they have, had a, a, a, a, a, a youngster's there was interested in music. And the pastor, he stood for all the instruments. Mm-hmm. And he got all the instruments on his name, issued them out to each member that wanted to, you know, interested enough to, uh, play the music. That is, interested enough in music in life. Mm-hmm. So, therefore, I got a violin. That's, that's what they gave me, a violin. Mm-hmm. And from there, I take an instructions from Professor Taylor. Mm-hmm. He gave me instructions on the violin.
Mm-hmm.

Well, I played that for a while. Then later on, that, uh, fellas began falling out. Nice we had supposed to have had instructions. Fellas began having dates, you know. Couldn't come out to rehearsal, uh, instructions. So, therefore, that, uh, caused the band to disband, see. And, uh, from that, well, the fellas went astray. And, uh, I wonder if you can hear me. Yeah. Mm-hmm. So, therefore, that's, uh, that's where I started music, and from the church, on the violin. What instrument did you take? And you must have had another instrument after the violin. Yeah, after the violin, I played that for a little while. Yeah, I take an instruction on, uh, Professor Taylor, and later on the Professor Correa. Yeah, but you changed from violin. And, uh, from the violin, I changed to banjo. Mm-hmm. Which my wife, she made the present of a banjo, and... Which I take great interest in, and I bought myself a mortal method, and that is, taught myself how to play the banjo. Mm-hmm. And you can still play it, huh? Uh, yes, I still know a little of it. I'm not accustomed, I'm not practical to it like I used to be. But, although, I still understand it. What year you took up the banjo about? Around 25. Mm-hmm. Yeah, 25. And I played a... You were grown? Oh, quite naturally. I was 17 when I... And 21, so therefore, 25, uh, quite... Four years different. But anyway, that, uh... I played the banjo about four... About nine years. About nine to ten years. Then, I gave that up. And later, a friend was interested in me learning some other instrument. So, it was an alto saxophone. Mm-hmm. And I tried that for a while. Gave me some, you know, ideas of it. I like myself on it. On the alto sax. Then, later on, we, uh... I went on through playing with different fellows with the alto. Played with old man Jackson, the bass player. You remember him? Mm-hmm. We had a band, and... Is that Eddie Jackson? Eddie Jackson, yes. String bass at that band, or... Oh, he was playing the sousaphone. Mm-hmm. Yeah. And we played different places. As I played in the alto. And, uh, also Luce, I think Luce played with us too, if I'm not mistaken. Which Luce is that? That's, uh, Albert Jackson. Oh, Luce. Yeah. Oh, Luce, yeah. Mm-hmm. So, therefore, that, uh... I played with so many different fellows, and doing the WPA band. Of course, I played in that band too. Mm-hmm. From about 1934 to about 19... Say within all, the 41. Which saxophone did you play with them? Well, I played both. I played, uh... I played soprano, yeah. I played soprano sax. In fact, when I first got on there, I didn't have any instrument at all. Mm-hmm. I gave up all the playing during that time. That's during around about 1934. Mm-hmm. During that time, well, I had some misfortune during my labor. Oh, yeah. I was working for the bank. I worked for the bank for about, uh, 11 years. 1933, the bank closed down. Mm-hmm. And, 34 was a tough year for me. See, and I didn't have no instrument or nothing. And, most likely, that I, uh, picked up on... That is, they told me about this WPA band. And, which I got... I... That is, I registered in this WPA. And, so the fellow told me I had to have an instrument. So, I borrowed an instrument from a friend, which was an album. I mean, the soprano sax. That's all he had to line me. So, I went on in there as soprano sax player. I played that. So, it was one of those curved sopranos. So, later on, when I made a payday, I bought my own soprano. So, therefore, I played the soprano, straight soprano. Throughout the WPA up until about 1930... 36, I think it was. 1936. Then, later on, I got to be a tenor. Mm-hmm. See, and I played tenor in the WPA band. When did you get with the Eureka? Well, around 1944, I think. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I was 44. I joined... I was playing with T-Boy. T-Boy was the leader of the Eureka brass band. 38. Rami T-Boy. And, he asked me to play with him. I was playing at a nightclub with him. And, he asked me to play with him. I had never played with a brass band. I mean a film band, you know. And, he asked me to play with him. So, I started playing with him. And, from then on, up to now, I'm still playing with him. And, and... Had you played any parades with the brass bands before? No, I had never played any parades or fumes with any other bands. Neither fumes or parades. No. Oh, that's amazing that you can do that. Uh-huh. What about, uh... When did you take up the clarin? I was always curious about that. Well... Mr. Russell. Bill Russell. He, uh... He, uh... He, he was interested in my... I don't know. He considered that, uh, technical fingering on the teller. Seemed like he felt as though that I could be much greater on the, on a clarinet. Uh, clarinet. So, he, him and another fellow came to a place where I was playing across the river at the fireman hall and he asked me. Uh, the fellow came up and asked me, say, look, if I give you a clarinet, I said, he'd say, would you try to learn it? And I'd say, well, I, I don't know. I'd say, it's pretty late in years to try to learn a clarinet. I'd say, an instrument like that, you'd have to raise up with it. And I'd come up with it in order to master it, uh, get enough out of it that it would entertain the people. So, therefore, that... Yeah. Okay. So, therefore, that, uh... So, later on, uh, I say it's too old now. I don't think I'd be interested in it. So, I just gave, you know, just like, I don't know, that's that. So, later on, him and Raph came to my house and brought the clarinet. Raph Collins, yeah. And, uh, they brought it to my house and, uh, he said, well, we brought you one. He said, it's up to you now. He said, it's up to you. He's up to you. Try to learn it. Yeah, element system. Yeah, element system, yeah. So, I said, well, I'll try to do the best that I can. So, what happened, I did. I tried. So, that'd been about three, a little better than three years ago. Off and on. You see, I played a little bit, play with a little bit. I tried. Never did take no instructions on it. Whatsoever. Just called to the line and said, I... You know, got some books or something. I like that, Belgium, St. Mary. Yes, uh-huh. Just picked it up. That's all. Anything else. What about, uh, how long you been with Thomas? Oh, since about around the same time. Around about, like, 44, 45, something like that. Mm-hmm. Yes, because I was working... Not steady, though, huh? Study, yeah. It was pretty steady then. Because I was working during the day at the Naval Supply, right on the river on Napoleon Avenue. I was working there. I was working about 12 hours a day there, and then I'd leave, bring my everything that I had right there, and I'd leave my instrument over across the river. I'd leave from there and go to work across the river right there at the Napoleon Ferry. And we used to work from 10 to 12 hours a day, and I'd be still working with Thomas about three nights a week. Mm-hmm. Yeah, I'd work with him a long time. A very long time. You can read, huh? All the guys... Well, consider it, I did read. I liked to read, yeah, but as he has been past, you know, lots of music I'd forgotten. Yeah. It comes back to you, I noticed. Yeah, it comes back to me, but so little that I had to use it, you know, that just causes you to forget. Well, I noticed you got the sheet music on Jebouzaam. Oh, yeah, yeah. Well, I just... Okay. That's it, I'm afraid. Time's running out. We all right, huh? Yeah. We all right. We all right.
All right, we're rolling. What's your name?
Lewis Hall Nelson Sr.
I see. And where were you born?
Born here in New Orleans, 1419, 2 Road Street, September 17, 1902.
And what about your family? Did anybody in your family play?
Yes, my mother played. My father, he played all. So my mother, she was a graduate from the Boston Conservatory of Music. She was a pianist.
And your father, what did he do?
He played all around the church and he was a medical doctor.
Did he read music? He studied, huh, too? Yes, yes. Didn't you have a brother, too?
Yes, he played saxophone a little.
What was his name?
George H. Nelson. I see.
And did you spend your early childhood in New Orleans?
No, I left New Orleans when I was about two months old. Went to a place out in the country named Napoleonville. I spent about 25 years out there.
Did they have any bands out there in the Polandville? Yes.

They had Clayman Williams and they had Joseph Garber. Clayman Williams, Professor Williams, he taught me the trombone. My mother, she wanted me to play piano. But I'd rather play the trombone. I liked the trombone better than I did the piano.
Mm-hmm. Did they have any trombones out there you were in the...
Yes, they had a fellow by the name of Lawrence Johnson. He was playing with a band out there. And they left to go to Lake Charles, Louisiana. And I said I always wanted to play a trombone like him.
Do you play like him today?
No, pretty close. He played smooth and he could play rough and he could play jazz. Mm-hmm. Try to get off and things like that, yes.
What was your first band you played with?

Joseph Garber was out in the country, out in the Polandville. Then I came to New Orleans. My first wife, she died. And that's when I met Kit Harris. Kit Harris, yes. And I played with him. And one night I was at the Bulls. And I met Sidney Desvene and I started playing with him.
What kind of band did Kit Harris have?
Oh, he had a little Dixieland. About six, seven pieces.
Was it different from the Joe Garber.
Oh, yes, it was. Joe Garber didn't have a Dixieland. He played mostly stocks and arrangements.
So you read and...
Yes.
Play that. And then Joe Harris got you started on something else, huh?
Who is that?
I say Kit Harris.

Kit Harris. I mean, you got you started on something else. Yes, yes. I came and started playing with him, yes. Then after I went to Sidney Desvene, and I was quite a young man. I was in my 20s, late 20s, rather. And I started playing with him. We used to play at the Bulls for the culling on Tuesdays, and play at the Pethean Temple, or the Roof Garden for the culling on Mondays. And all the rest of the week, we was playing for the White. All the leading clubs out in the city of New Orleans, like the Southern Yacht, Jewish Country Club, New Orleans Country Club, Colonial Country Club, all the leading hotels in the city of New Orleans. We'd go in every night.
What kind of trombone did you play with Desvene?
Well, I had to play this modern trombone, you know, read music and play sweet solos and arrangements.
Well, who took the hots with a...
Well, he didn't feature much hots on trombone. I played the hots if he'd write the parts that far.
But you didn't fake much with him?
No, it was just strictly reading.
Did Kit Harris fake at all?
Oh, yes, yes. He read and he faked. We had to fake with him. That's where I learned the faking.
That's where you got...

So after Sidney Desvene and Brand broke up, then I had to just come back to this Dick's land. I knew the chords, and the punch, you know, the chords is all the same. I knew all the pieces, because I heard them play it. I used to play it then. I played with Kid Renier. Played with Punch. I didn't play with Buddy Petit, because I was old enough, but at the time he was here, and I was in the country. I could have played with him. I used to go play with Jim Robinson. He was playing with a band at the Levita. That was a jetty dance.
I used to rest him up. No, yeah.

Just rest him up. Give him a break, because they played from eight until. Peace continues. As soon as one stopped, they didn't speak of another piece. You know, so those men get rid of the tickets. You buy tickets to jetty dance.
People must love to play then. Yes. To do all that sitting in and rest people up, you know.
Yeah.
Well, I think we're just about run out of time on this. You just want a little sketch of your life.
That's perfectly all right. I thank you very much. You're perfectly welcome, Mr. Allen. It's a pleasure talking with you.
Thank you.
Thank you.
